title: The Band Isn’t the Load
subtitle: To make resistance-band training easier to repeat and progress, log the setup—not just the color.
imageAlt: Two friends doing separate resistance-band exercises in a bright living room, each using a different band setup and comparing notes in a small training log.
imageConcept: A relaxed, realistic scene of two friends training in a bright living room: one performs a band row from a secure door anchor while the other does a standing press, with a notebook open nearby showing grip positions and repetitions. The focus is on their individual setups and shared attention, not on a dramatic pose or matching equipment.
body: The same band can be a different exercise

You pick up a familiar band, take your usual stance and begin a row. It feels harder than last time. Maybe you are tired; maybe your grip moved a few inches; maybe you started with the band already more stretched. The color printed on the band has not changed, but the conditions have. That is why “three sets with the red band” is an incomplete training record. It tells you what you did in broad strokes, not necessarily how you did it. For resistance-band work, the setup is part of the resistance: where the band begins, where it is attached, how you hold it and how far you move all help determine the challenge. A better record does not need a force gauge or an elaborate spreadsheet. It needs enough detail to help you make a fair comparison next time.
Color is a label, not a universal load

Band colors are useful for identifying equipment, but they are not a reliable conversion chart to a precise weight. Measurements of color-coded Thera-Band products found that tension values differed from manufacturer reference values for five colors. [1] The force produced also changes as a band is stretched; the color alone cannot tell you the force at every point in a repetition. [1] Researchers have measured particular bands at standardized lengths and stretches, then developed equations for those specific conditions. That is valuable work, but it does not create a universal “blue equals this many pounds” rule for every band, anchor and grip. [2] In practice, treat a color as a way to identify one item in your kit. Record the item and its setup, and avoid describing band resistance as an exact weight equivalent unless you have a valid measurement for that specific arrangement.
Build a log that answers the useful question

A training log should help you answer: Can I repeat this setup, and did I make a deliberate change? For each movement, write down the exercise, the band or its identifying color and brand, the anchor point, your starting position or grip, the range of motion, and the number of repetitions and sets. Add a short note about effort if helpful—for example, “last two reps challenging, movement controlled.” That note is a personal observation, not a measurement of force. You might record a row as: “Standing row; green loop; anchored at chest height; feet on tape marks; hands at marked grip points; pull to ribs; 3 × 10.” A phone note or paper card is enough. The goal is not to log every detail of your life. It is to capture the few variables that would otherwise drift between sessions, so a later change means something.
Make progression one change at a time

When you want a set to become more challenging, first decide what you will change. You could use a different band, shorten the starting length, adjust your grip, alter your stance or increase repetitions. Change one variable, then record it. If you shorten your grip and add reps in the same session, you may still have a good workout, but you will not know which adjustment changed the feel. A clean comparison might be: same anchor, range and repetitions; hands moved one marked position farther from the anchor. Or: same setup, one extra repetition per set. Keep the movement controlled and use a range that feels appropriate for you. If the band slips, the anchor shifts or the movement becomes difficult to control, stop and reset rather than trying to push through a compromised setup. This is practical record-keeping, not a requirement to chase a number every workout.
A repeatable setup starts before the first rep

Choose a stable anchor intended for the task, and follow the band and anchor maker’s instructions. Before you begin, check the band for visible damage and make sure its path is clear of sharp edges. Set your position, then note landmarks that can be found again: feet on floor seams, a chair behind you, a particular door anchor position or a grip mark. For a floor-based exercise, note where your body starts; for a standing exercise, note your distance from the anchor and whether the band is slack or already under tension at the start. These details do not make the force perfectly measurable, but they make the session more repeatable. If you cannot safely recreate the anchor or position, do not treat the next session as a direct comparison. Choose a secure arrangement and make a fresh baseline instead.
Train together without turning it into a contest

Two people can follow the same plan and use different setups. One friend might do a band press with a shorter starting length and six repetitions; another might choose a longer length and ten. Those are not competing scores. Bodies, training histories, comfort and goals differ, and a band color does not rank anyone’s effort. A shared log can show each person’s own setup and next step while keeping the movement consistent enough to learn from. For example, both partners can use the same anchor and exercise, then each mark a comfortable grip position and record their own reps. If one person is learning the movement, they can begin with a setup that allows a smooth, controlled range and build familiarity before changing the challenge. Research comparing elastic and conventional resistance found no superiority of one method for strength gains across the included studies; the results support their potential to produce similar gains under the studied protocols, not a claim that every program or setup is interchangeable. [3]

A band log is not a lab instrument, and it does not need to be. Its value is that it helps distinguish a real training adjustment from an accidental one. Use the same movement and repeatable landmarks for a few sessions; note how many controlled repetitions you complete and how the set feels. When that becomes manageable, choose one change and write it down. If the new setup feels too difficult to control, return to the previous one or make a smaller adjustment. If you are managing pain, returning from injury or unsure which movements suit you, seek individualized guidance from a qualified health or rehabilitation professional. The wider strength-training evidence also does not make a particular band setup mandatory: elastic resistance is one option among several, and equipment type alone is not the whole program. A useful session is one you can perform safely, repeat and adapt to your own needs. The color is the label. Your recorded setup is the comparison.
